question.text: Ms. Priya Shah of Saraswati Capital is explaining the Random Walk Hypothesis to a new analyst. Which statement correctly describes the Random Walk model as the early foundation of the Efficient Market Hypothesis?

answer.text: Successive one-period returns are perfectly negatively correlated, so mean reversion always exists.
Successive one-period returns are independent and identically distributed, implying changes in security prices occur randomly.
Prices follow a deterministic trend with a known drift plus a periodic calendar effect.
Returns on any day are a linear function of the prior 5-day moving average.

explanation.text: The Logic: Per Ch 3.2, the early treatment of efficient markets was built on the Random Walk Hypothesis - successive one-period returns are independent and identically distributed, implying price changes occur randomly. Fama (1970) later formalised this into the three forms of EMH. The Trap: Option A invokes mean reversion (an anomaly) - the opposite of random walk. Option C describes a calendar-effect model. Option D is essentially a moving-average forecast, inconsistent with independence. Cross-Exam Context: XXI-B (PM) and XV (Research Analyst) test this at similar depth. Bachelier's 1900 thesis on speculation and Fama's 1970 JoF paper are canonical references across all NISM market-theory chapters. Manager's Pro-Tip: As a manager, even if you believe your deal-sourcing is non-random, frame LP discussions around WHY your alpha is not a random walk - private information asymmetry, negotiated terms, operational value creation.
